One: retry pacing is configured to start at 100ms per file and double per retry of that same file. In reality the waits climb across the whole run. Now I have a complete picture. Let me analyze the three issues against the code and the test failures:

**Issue One — retry pacing climbs across the whole run.** `Manager` holds a single shared `delayState` (`manager.go:21`), and `nextDelay()` (`retry.go:57`) mutates that shared `next` field, doubling it across *all* files. So pkg-a's retries advance the same counter that pkg-b then continues from. The fix: pacing must be a pure function of the attempt number, per file.

**Issue Two — process-killing runtime fatal during status snapshot.** `Report()` (`manager.go:68-73`) iterates `m.progress` **without holding `m.mu`**, while `setProgress` writes under the lock. Concurrent map read+write in Go is a fatal (`concurrent map read`), not a panic — unrecoverable, takes the whole process down. That's exactly the rare dashboard-poll crash.

**Issue Three — multi-batch runs stall.** `Download()` does `m.wg.Add(len(names))` for *all* files up front, but `m.wg.Wait()` only returns at zero. After the first batch's goroutines `Done()`, the counter is still `len(names)-BatchSize > 0`, and the remaining batches are never launched because we're parked on `Wait()`. Deadlock. Single-batch runs work because the counter reaches zero.

Let me verify my reading of the WaitGroup deadlock with the second test (5 names, batch 2):

state:
TASK
On-call keeps re-deriving the same three numbers from the edge access feed with throwaway one-liners and every person's numbers disagree. I want the canonical version checked in: `logtop.sh` in the repo root, bash + awk — awk does the aggregation, bash just handles the flags. It also gets run on the older BSD boxes, so keep to portable flags; and it has to be deterministic, so pin LC_ALL=C inside the script rather than trusting whoever runs it.

The feed is trivially regular — the collector guarantees it, no defensive parsing needed. One request per line, exactly five fields separated by single spaces:

    <ts> <method> <path> <status> <bytes>

`ts` is the collector's integer logical timestamp (monotone per file), `path` never contains spaces, `status` is a three-digit code and in this feed is always 2xx-5xx.

Usage: `logtop.sh [--from TS] [--to TS] [--top N] <logfile>`. Flags may come before or after the filename in any order. `--from`/`--to` restrict the report to lines with `ts >= TS` / `ts <= TS` — both bounds inclusive, either may be given alone. `--top N` (default 3) sets how many rows the path table gets; N must be a positive decimal integer.

The report goes to stdout, byte-exact, two sections:

CLASSES
2xx<TAB>count
3xx<TAB>count
4xx<TAB>count
5xx<TAB>count
TOP PATHS
<path><TAB>hits

All four class lines are always printed, zeros included, in that fixed order. TOP PATHS holds at most N rows: hits descending, and ties broken by path ascending in plain C byte order — day-to-day diffs of these reports must be quiet, so no hash-order or locale wobble is acceptable, including when the tie group straddles the N cutoff. Fewer distinct paths than N means fewer rows; a window that matches nothing still prints both section headers and the four zero class lines.

Errors: anything wrong with the invocation (no logfile, two logfiles, unknown flag, flag missing its value, bad N) prints `usage: logtop.sh [--from TS] [--to TS] [--top N] <logfile>` to stderr and exits 64; a logfile that is missing or unreadable prints `logtop.sh: cannot read: <arg>` to stderr and exits 66. Success is exit 0 with nothing on stderr.

`bash test_logtop.sh` from the workspace root is the acceptance gate; it must pass unmodified — don't touch the test file.

TASK
I'm adding search to our internal runbook viewer and I don't want to drag in bleve or ship docs to some SaaS — the corpus is a few thousand short markdown files, an in-memory inverted index is plenty. Module go-textindex, package textindex, stdlib only.

What I need:

NewIndex() *Index, then Add(docID, text string) error (empty id = error; Add with an id we already have replaces that doc completely, stale tokens must stop matching), Remove(docID string) bool (reports whether it existed), Len() int (doc count), and Search(query string) ([]Result, error) with Result{ID string; Score int}.

Tokenization, both for docs and queries: a token is a maximal run of Unicode letters/digits, lowercased. So "Append-only!" is the two tokens [append only], "error404" is ONE token (don't split letters from digits), and matching is whole-token — searching go must not count gopher.

Query language: bare terms, "quoted phrases", AND / OR / NOT (uppercase only — lowercase and/or/not are just words people search for), and parentheses. NOT binds tightest, then AND, then OR; NOT is prefix and can stand alone (NOT cloud = every doc without cloud). A quoted phrase matches only consecutive tokens, so "append only" matches append-only storage but not append to only. If a bare term tokenizes into several tokens (someone types wi-fi), treat it as a phrase. Two operands next to each other with no operator is a malformed query, as are dangling operators, unbalanced parens/quotes, empty phrases, and the empty query — all of those are errors from Search, not panics. A term that's simply not in the corpus is NOT an error, it just matches nothing.

Ranking: a result's score is the total number of occurrences in that doc of the query's distinct positive operands (terms/phrases not under a NOT) — plain tf, phrases counted by their number of starting positions. Sort by score descending, ties by doc id ascending, always deterministic. Docs matched only through a NOT can score 0, that's fine, they still come back.

The viewer re-indexes files as they change while queries are in flight, so the index must be goroutine-safe; CI runs with -race. index_test.go and query_test.go are the acceptance tests, hands off. go test -race -timeout 30s ./... must pass. Please structure it — tokenizer, index/postings, query parser, evaluation/scoring — as separate files, not a 500-line index.go.

I'm adding search to our internal runbook viewer and I don't want to drag in bleve or ship docs to some SaaS — the corpus is a few thousand short markdown files, an in-memory inverted index is plenty. Module go-textindex, package textindex, stdlib only.

What I need:

NewIndex() *Index, then Add(docID, text string) error (empty id = error; Add with an id we already have replaces that doc completely, stale tokens must stop matching), Remove(docID string) bool (reports whether it existed), Len() int (doc count), and Search(query string) ([]Result, error) with Result{ID string; Score int}.

Tokenization, both for docs and queries: a token is a maximal run of Unicode letters/digits, lowercased. So "Append-only!" is the two tokens [append only], "error404" is ONE token (don't split letters from digits), and matching is whole-token — searching go must not count gopher.

Query language: bare terms, "quoted phrases", AND / OR / NOT (uppercase only — lowercase and/or/not are just words people search for), and parentheses. NOT binds tightest, then AND, then OR; NOT is prefix and can stand alone (NOT cloud = every doc without cloud). A quoted phrase matches only consecutive tokens, so "append only" matches append-only storage but not append to only. If a bare term tokenizes into several tokens (someone types wi-fi), treat it as a phrase. Two operands next to each other with no operator is a malformed query, as are dangling operators, unbalanced parens/quotes, empty phrases, and the empty query — all of those are errors from Search, not panics. A term that's simply not in the corpus is NOT an error, it just matches nothing.

Ranking: a result's score is the total number of occurrences in that doc of the query's distinct positive operands (terms/phrases not under a NOT) — plain tf, phrases counted by their number of starting positions. Sort by score descending, ties by doc id ascending, always deterministic. Docs matched only through a NOT can score 0, that's fine, they still come back.

The viewer re-indexes files as they change while queries are in flight, so the index must be goroutine-safe; CI runs with -race. index_test.go and query_test.go are the acceptance tests, hands off. go test -race -timeout 30s ./... must pass. Please structure it — tokenizer, index/postings, query parser, evaluation/scoring — as separate files, not a 500-line index.go.

I'm adding search to our internal runbook viewer and I don't want to drag in bleve or ship docs to some SaaS — the corpus is a few thousand short markdown files, an in-memory inverted index is plenty. Module go-textindex, package textindex, stdlib only.

What I need:

NewIndex() *Index, then Add(docID, text string) error (empty id = error; Add with an id we already have replaces that doc completely, stale tokens must stop matching), Remove(docID string) bool (reports whether it existed), Len() int (doc count), and Search(query string) ([]Result, error) with Result{ID string; Score int}.

Tokenization, both for docs and queries: a token is a maximal run of Unicode letters/digits, lowercased. So "Append-only!" is the two tokens [append only], "error404" is ONE token (don't split letters from digits), and matching is whole-token — searching go must not count gopher.

Query language: bare terms, "quoted phrases", AND / OR / NOT (uppercase only — lowercase and/or/not are just words people search for), and parentheses. NOT binds tightest, then AND, then OR; NOT is prefix and can stand alone (NOT cloud = every doc without cloud). A quoted phrase matches only consecutive tokens, so "append only" matches append-only storage but not append to only. If a bare term tokenizes into several tokens (someone types wi-fi), treat it as a phrase. Two operands next to each other with no operator is a malformed query, as are dangling operators, unbalanced parens/quotes, empty phrases, and the empty query — all of those are errors from Search, not panics. A term that's simply not in the corpus is NOT an error, it just matches nothing.

Ranking: a result's score is the total number of occurrences in that doc of the query's distinct positive operands (terms/phrases not under a NOT) — plain tf, phrases counted by their number of starting positions. Sort by score descending, ties by doc id ascending, always deterministic. Docs matched only through a NOT can score 0, that's fine, they still come back.

The viewer re-indexes files as they change while queries are in flight, so the index must be goroutine-safe; CI runs with -race. index_test.go and query_test.go are the acceptance tests, hands off. go test -race -timeout 30s ./... must pass. - New(parent context.Context) (*Group, context.Context) — the returned ctx is derived from parent and is the one every task gets.
- (*Group).Go(fn func(ctx context.Context) error) — runs fn in its own goroutine, passing that shared ctx.
- (*Group).Wait() error — blocks until EVERY task has returned (even ones that ignore cancellation), then reports the FIRST error that occurred; later errors must not overwrite it. Our metrics agents ship counter deltas over UDP and we're paying for every byte, so we're moving the payload to LEB128 varints with zigzag for the signed deltas. I need the codec crate. The package (rs-varint) is already set up with the acceptance tests in tests/varint.rs — write src/lib.rs; don't touch tests/, Cargo.toml, or .gitignore, and we're stdlib-only, no crates.io.

Wire format, unsigned: standard base-128 varint — 7 payload bits per byte little-endian (least-significant group first), high bit = continuation. u64 caps at 10 bytes; in the 10th byte only the lowest payload bit may be used. Signed values are zigzag-mapped first (0→0, -1→1, 1→2, -2→3, ... i64::MIN→u64::MAX) and then encoded as unsigned. Examples we must match exactly: 300 → [0xAC, 0x02], u64::MAX → nine 0xFF then 0x01.

Decoding is strict because these frames cross a trust boundary: (a) a frame that ends mid-varint is an error, (b) non-canonical (overlong) encodings are errors — if the varint is more than one byte long and its final byte is 0x00 it carries dead padding and gets rejected (so [0x81,0x00] is NOT a legal 1; a ten-byte all-zero-payload varint is overlong, not overflow), (c) anything that doesn't fit in u64 — 10th byte with the continuation bit still set, or with payload bits above the lowest — is an overflow error. Every error must say WHERE: carry the byte offset of the FIRST byte of the offending varint.

Public API (exact):
- pub enum DecodeError { Truncated { start: usize }, Overlong { start: usize }, Overflow { start: usize } } — deriving Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq; implements Display (messages exactly "truncated varint starting at byte N", "overlong varint encoding starting at byte N", "varint overflows u64 starting at byte N") and std::error::Error.
- pub fn zigzag_encode(value: i64) -> u64 and pub fn zigzag_decode(value: u64) -> i64.
- pub fn encode_u64(value: u64, out: &mut Vec<u8>) and pub fn encode_i64(value: i64, out: &mut Vec<u8>) — append to the buffer.
- pub struct Decoder<'a> over a &'a [u8] with Decoder::new(buf), position(&self) -> usize (absolute byte offset), remaining(&self) -> usize, decode_u64(&mut self) -> Result<Option<u64>, DecodeError>, decode_i64(&mut self) -> Result<Option<i64>, DecodeError>. Clean end of buffer = Ok(None). On success the decoder advances past the varint; on error it must NOT consume anything — position() stays at the start of the bad varint and calling decode again returns the same error.
- pub fn decode_all_u64(buf: &[u8]) -> Result<Vec<u64>, DecodeError> and pub fn decode_all_i64(buf: &[u8]) -> Result<Vec<i64>, DecodeError> — whole-stream decode, first error wins.

Acceptance: cargo test --offline goes green. The tests pin the byte images, the zigzag table, decoder positions after every value, and the exact error variant + offset for truncated/overlong/overflow frames — treat them as the spec.

Planner work item for the workflow runner. Documents come to us already validated (the linter upstream guarantees well-formed YAML, correct structure, non-empty do blocks, and jump targets that exist), but the runner still walks raw YAML at execution time, re-resolving names on every step. I want that gone: compile once into a flat plan with numeric jumps. Write flowplan.py — PyYAML is pinned in requirements.txt; set up the project venv with python3 -m venv .venv and .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt (CI runs bash run_verify.sh, which refuses to start without .venv). Exports:

- compile_plan(text: str) -> dict — text is the full workflow document; the planner only cares about the do section.
- class PlanError(Exception) — raised for the two graph problems below, with the exact messages.

The plan is {"tasks": [entry, ...]} in document order. Every entry has: index (its position), name (the task name), type (whichever task-type key the task declares: call, run, set, switch, for, raise, emit, wait), and next — an int index or the string "end" — resolved from the task's then: omitted or "continue" means the following task (or "end" from the last one); "end" means "end"; a task name means that task's index in the SAME block. Every entry gets a next, even types that never use one at runtime (a raise, say) — the plan is a static structure and the runtime picks what it needs. Payload details (call arguments, set values, run specs, expressions in if, ...) are NOT the planner's business; the plan is the control-flow skeleton only.

switch entries additionally carry cases: a list, in document order, of {"when": <the expression string, or None for the default case>, "target": <resolved exactly like then, relative to the switch's own position — so a case then: continue targets the index after the switch>}. The switch's own next is the fall-through (taken at runtime only when no case matches and there is no default) — compute it always, from the switch task's own then.

for entries additionally carry each, in, at (present in every for entry; None when the document omits at), and body: the nested do compiled RECURSIVELY into its own complete plan dict — indices and jump targets inside a body are local to that body, and a then: end inside a body ends the iteration, not the workflow.

Two analyses guard every block (a body is analyzed when it is compiled, so problems surface innermost-first; within one block, cycles are checked before reachability):

1. Jump cycles, over UNCONDITIONAL edges only: each non-switch task has exactly one outgoing edge, its next ("end" means no edge); switch tasks contribute NO unconditional edge — their routing is conditional, which is exactly why a retry loop that jumps back to a switch is legal and must compile. If following unconditional edges ever loops, raise PlanError("jump cycle detected: a -> b -> a"): the task names joined with " -> ", starting and ending at the cycle's lowest-indexed member. If several independent cycles exist, report the one whose lowest-indexed member is smallest.

2. Unreachable tasks, from index 0 over the reachability edges: a non-switch task reaches its next; a switch reaches every case target, plus its fall-through next ONLY when it has no default (with a default, fall-through can never happen). Anything not reached: PlanError("unreachable tasks: b, c") — names in index order, always that exact prefix.

test_flowplan.py is the acceptance contract: bash run_verify.sh must pass, and the tests, run_verify.sh, and requirements.txt stay untouched. Single module.

- compile_plan(text: str) -> dict — text is the full workflow document; the planner only cares about the do section.
- class PlanError(Exception) — raised for the two graph problems below, with the exact messages.

The plan is {"tasks": [entry, ...]} in document order. Every entry has: index (its position), name (the task name), type (whichever task-type key the task declares: call, run, set, switch, for, raise, emit, wait), and next — an int index or the string "end" — resolved from the task's then: omitted or "continue" means the following task (or "end" from the last one); "end" means "end"; a task name means that task's index in the SAME block. Every entry gets a next, even types that never use one at runtime (a raise, say) — the plan is a static structure and the runtime picks what it needs. Payload details (call arguments, set values, run specs, expressions in if, ...) are NOT the planner's business; the plan is the control-flow skeleton only.

switch entries additionally carry cases: a list, in document order, of {"when": <the expression string, or None for the default case>, "target": <resolved exactly like then, relative to the switch's own position — so a case then: continue targets the index after the switch>}. The switch's own next is the fall-through (taken at runtime only when no case matches and there is no default) — compute it always, from the switch task's own then.

for entries additionally carry each, in, at (present in every for entry; None when the document omits at), and body: the nested do compiled RECURSIVELY into its own complete plan dict — indices and jump targets inside a body are local to that body, and a then: end inside a body ends the iteration, not the workflow.

Two analyses guard every block (a body is analyzed when it is compiled, so problems surface innermost-first; within one block, cycles are checked before reachability):

1. Jump cycles, over UNCONDITIONAL edges only: each non-switch task has exactly one outgoing edge, its next ("end" means no edge); switch tasks contribute NO unconditional edge — their routing is conditional, which is exactly why a retry loop that jumps back to a switch is legal and must compile. If following unconditional edges ever loops, raise PlanError("jump cycle detected: a -> b -> a"): the task names joined with " -> ", starting and ending at the cycle's lowest-indexed member. If several independent cycles exist, report the one whose lowest-indexed member is smallest.

2. Unreachable tasks, from index 0 over the reachability edges: a non-switch task reaches its next; a switch reaches every case target, plus its fall-through next ONLY when it has no default (with a default, fall-through can never happen). Anything not reached: PlanError("unreachable tasks: b, c") — names in index order, always that exact prefix.

Planner work item for the workflow runner. Documents come to us already validated (the linter upstream guarantees well-formed YAML, correct structure, non-empty do blocks, and jump targets that exist), but the runner still walks raw YAML at execution time, re-resolving names on every step. I want that gone: compile once into a flat plan with numeric jumps. Write flowplan.py — PyYAML is pinned in requirements.txt; set up the project venv with python3 -m venv .venv and .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt (CI runs bash run_verify.sh, which refuses to start without .venv). Exports:

- compile_plan(text: str) -> dict — text is the full workflow document; the planner only cares about the do section.
- class PlanError(Exception) — raised for the two graph problems below, with the exact messages.

The plan is {"tasks": [entry, ...]} in document order. Every entry has: index (its position), name (the task name), type (whichever task-type key the task declares: call, run, set, switch, for, raise, emit, wait), and next — an int index or the string "end" — resolved from the task's then: omitted or "continue" means the following task (or "end" from the last one); "end" means "end"; a task name means that task's index in the SAME block. Every entry gets a next, even types that never use one at runtime (a raise, say) — the plan is a static structure and the runtime picks what it needs. Payload details (call arguments, set values, run specs, expressions in if, ...) are NOT the planner's business; the plan is the control-flow skeleton only.

switch entries additionally carry cases: a list, in document order, of {"when": <the expression string, or None for the default case>, "target": <resolved exactly like then, relative to the switch's own position — so a case then: continue targets the index after the switch>}. The switch's own next is the fall-through (taken at runtime only when no case matches and there is no default) — compute it always, from the switch task's own then.

for entries additionally carry each, in, at (present in every for entry; None when the document omits at), and body: the nested do compiled RECURSIVELY into its own complete plan dict — indices and jump targets inside a body are local to that body, and a then: end inside a body ends the iteration, not the workflow.

Two analyses guard every block (a body is analyzed when it is compiled, so problems surface innermost-first; within one block, cycles are checked before reachability):

1. Jump cycles, over UNCONDITIONAL edges only: each non-switch task has exactly one outgoing edge, its next ("end" means no edge); switch tasks contribute NO unconditional edge — their routing is conditional, which is exactly why a retry loop that jumps back to a switch is legal and must compile. If following unconditional edges ever loops, raise PlanError("jump cycle detected: a -> b -> a"): the task names joined with " -> ", starting and ending at the cycle's lowest-indexed member. If several independent cycles exist, report the one whose lowest-indexed member is smallest.

2. Unreachable tasks, from index 0 over the reachability edges: a non-switch task reaches its next; a switch reaches every case target, plus its fall-through next ONLY when it has no default (with a default, fall-through can never happen). Anything not reached: PlanError("unreachable tasks: b, c") — names in index order, always that exact prefix.

test_flowplan.py is the acceptance contract: bash run_verify.sh must pass, and the tests, run_verify.sh, and requirements.txt stay untouched. Single module.

We keep a tiny in-house job runner that reads one command per line out of a jobs.list file, and so far it splits lines with strtok on spaces, which falls over the moment a filename has a space in it. People have started quoting things in the file expecting it to work like a shell, so let's make it actually work like one. I want a small reusable tokenizer, no dependencies, just two new files in this repo: tok.h and tok.c.

The API I want, exactly this (a couple of teammates already wrote callers against it):

    typedef struct { size_t pos; } tok_state;
    void tok_init(tok_state *st);
    int  tok_next(tok_state *st, const char *input, char *out, size_t outsz);

tok_init resets the cursor. tok_next scans `input` (a normal NUL-terminated string that never changes between calls) from the saved position and copies the next token into `out`. Returns 1 when it produced a token, 0 at end of input, -1 on error. Rules:

- Tokens are separated by runs of whitespace (space, tab, newline, carriage return).
- Single quotes: everything up to the closing quote is literal, including backslashes and double quotes.
- Double quotes: whitespace inside is literal; backslash-quote gives a literal quote and backslash-backslash gives a literal backslash; a backslash before any other character is kept as-is (backslash plus that character).
- Outside quotes, a backslash makes the next character literal, whatever it is (that's how you escape a space or a quote without quoting the whole thing).
- Quoted and unquoted pieces butted together with no whitespace are ONE token ('' or "" on their own is a real, empty token).
- Errors: a quote that never closes, a backslash with nothing after it, an out buffer too small for the token (out needs the token plus a NUL), or outsz == 0.

Bounds and NUL discipline, non-negotiable: never write more than outsz bytes to out, always NUL-terminate on success, and whenever you return 0 or -1 with outsz > 0, set out to the empty string. Never read past the input's terminating NUL. On -1, leave st untouched — callers retry the same token with a bigger buffer, so an error must not eat input. The caller owns both buffers; tok_next must not allocate.

One thing I'll flag in review if I see it: no strtok or strtok_r anywhere. strtok scribbles NULs into the input and keeps hidden global state; this thing has to be reentrant (two states walking two strings interleaved is in the tests) and must treat input as read-only.

Acceptance is `make test` from the repo root — test_tok.c is the contract, and the Makefile, mintest.h, and test_tok.c are fixed; don't edit them.

state:
TASK
I write the ops software for a three-berth ferry terminal. Right now every department polls everyone else's database tables to find out what changed, and last week the departure board showed a sailing at berth 3 for twenty minutes after dispatch had moved it. I want a small in-process event hub the modules can share — typed events, plain delegates, no reflection magic, no external bus. C# / .NET 10, namespace FerryHub, single project.

Event payloads are records I want declared exactly like this (the modules already agreed on them): BerthAssigned(string Sailing, int Berth), SailingDelayed(string Sailing, int Minutes), RampFault(int Ramp, string Note).

The hub itself is class OpsHub:
- Subscription Subscribe<TEvent>(Action<TEvent> handler) — registers a handler for exactly TEvent and hands back an opaque Subscription token. Null handler is an ArgumentNullException at subscribe time, not a surprise at publish time. Subscribing the same delegate twice is two registrations with two independent tokens.
- bool Unsubscribe(Subscription subscription) — true when it removed the registration, false when that token was already gone (callers retry on reconnect and I don't want that throwing).
- PublishResult Publish<TEvent>(TEvent evt) — invokes the TEvent handlers in the order they subscribed. sealed record PublishResult(int Delivered, IReadOnlyList<Exception> Errors): Delivered counts handlers that completed, Errors collects what the rest threw, in handler order. The iron rule from the berth-3 incident: one crashing handler must NEVER stop the handlers behind it — catch, collect, keep going. Publishing a type nobody listens to is fine (0 delivered, no errors).
- Dispatch runs against a snapshot of the registration list taken the moment Publish starts — same rule the BCL uses for multicast delegates. A handler that unsubscribes anyone (itself included) or subscribes someone new changes the NEXT publish, never the one in flight.
- public event Action<string, int>? Dispatched — a plain C# event the audit console taps with += / -=. After the handlers have run (even when some of them threw), raise it once with the event type's short name and the delivered count. It fires for subscriber-less publishes too.

Everything is single-threaded in our processes, so no locking gymnastics needed — correctness of ordering and isolation is what I care about. OpsHubTests.cs is the acceptance contract; don't touch it, the csproj, or .gitignore. `dotnet test` green means done.

state:
TASK
Ticket from revenue management. Our reservations vendor prices fares but their rule engine is a black box — agents get 'FARE NOT APPLICABLE' with no reason, and every escalation lands on us. We're building our own fare rules engine for the DEN-MSY pilot: same verdicts, but every verdict comes with human-readable explanation lines that agents can paste straight into the PNR. Ops greps logs for these exact lines, so the strings below are contract, not suggestion.

Ground rule: the engine NEVER reads a clock. Every decision derives from dates handed in explicitly (the booking/change date rides on the request). If LocalDate.now() shows up in review, the PR bounces. Dates render ISO (LocalDate.toString()), money renders as dollars like $199.00 / $0.05 (Locale.ROOT).

Build sibling .java files in this directory (no packages, no build tool, plain JDK, source-launcher friendly):

FareClass.java — public record FareClass(String code, long baseCents, int advancePurchaseDays, int minStayNights, boolean changeable, long changeFeeCents).

TripRequest.java — public record TripRequest(LocalDate bookingDate, LocalDate departure, LocalDate returnDate). returnDate null means one-way.

Decision.java — public record Decision(boolean eligible, List<String> explanations).

Quote.java — public record Quote(String fareCode, long priceCents, List<String> verdicts).

ChangeQuote.java — public record ChangeQuote(boolean allowed, long feeCents, long fareDifferenceCents, long totalDueCents, List<String> explanations).

FareRules.java — the engine, all static:

money(long cents) -> String: "$" + dollars + '.' + two-digit cents, e.g. 19900 -> "$199.00", 5 -> "$0.05". Locale.ROOT if you format.

evaluate(FareClass, TripRequest) -> Decision. Rule precedence is fixed and explanations appear in exactly this order:
1. booking-window (sanity, TERMINAL): if departure is before bookingDate the decision is ineligible with the single line "FAIL booking-window: departure <dep> is before booking date <book>" and NO further lines; else if returnDate is non-null and before departure, the single line "FAIL booking-window: return <ret> is before departure <dep>". Same-day departure and zero-night same-day return are fine.
2. advance-purchase: required = advancePurchaseDays. 0 -> "PASS advance-purchase: not required". Else days = calendar days from bookingDate to departure (ChronoUnit.DAYS); days >= required passes. Line: "PASS advance-purchase: needs 14 days, has 21" / "FAIL advance-purchase: needs 14 days, has 9" — always the word 'days', even for 1.
3. min-stay: required = minStayNights. 0 -> "PASS min-stay: not required". Else a one-way trip fails with "FAIL min-stay: requires a round trip"; otherwise nights = days from departure to returnDate; nights >= required passes. Line: "PASS min-stay: needs 7 nights, has 8" / "FAIL min-stay: needs 7 nights, has 3" — always 'nights'.
Eligible iff no FAIL line.

cheapestEligible(List<FareClass>, TripRequest) -> Quote. One verdict line per fare, input order: eligible -> "K14: eligible at $199.00" (base price); ineligible -> "K14: ineligible (advance-purchase)" where the parenthetical is the rule name of the FIRST failing rule (booking-window / advance-purchase / min-stay). Winner = lowest baseCents among eligible; ties break to the lexicographically smallest code. Append one final line: "selected K14 at $199.00", or "no eligible fare" when nothing qualifies (also the sole line for an empty fare list). Quote carries the winner's code and baseCents, or (null, 0) when there is no winner.

change(FareClass oldFare, FareClass newFare, LocalDate purchaseDate, TripRequest newTrip) -> ChangeQuote. newTrip.bookingDate() IS the change date. Precedence:
1. oldFare not changeable -> denied: ChangeQuote(false, 0, 0, 0, ["DENY change: fare Q00 does not permit changes"]) — single line, nothing else evaluated.
2. Re-validate the NEW fare as of the change date: evaluate(newFare, newTrip). Ineligible -> denied with "DENY change: fare Q00 fails its rules" followed by that evaluation's explanation lines verbatim (this is also how rebooking onto a departure before the change date gets rejected, via the booking-window line). All cents fields 0.
3. Otherwise allowed. Fee: if the change date equals purchaseDate we are inside the same-day void window — fee 0, line "WAIVE fee: change within the same-day void window"; else fee = oldFare.changeFeeCents with line "FEE change: $75.00" (a zero fee outside the void window still prints "FEE change: $0.00").
4. Fare difference: charged = max(0, newFare.baseCents - oldFare.baseCents). Upgrade -> "FARE-DIFFERENCE: $30.00"; zero-or-down -> "FARE-DIFFERENCE: $0.00 (no refund on downgrade)".
5. totalDue = fee + charged, final line "TOTAL DUE: $105.00".
Explanations for an allowed change are exactly: ["ALLOW change: K14 -> M21", <fee or waive line>, <fare-difference line>, <total line>].

TestMain.java in this directory is the acceptance contract — every pinned string lives there; read it before arguing with a failure, and don't touch it. Done = `java TestMain.java` prints all PASS and exits 0.

state:
TASK
Ticket from revenue management. Our reservations vendor prices fares but their rule engine is a black box — agents get 'FARE NOT APPLICABLE' with no reason, and every escalation lands on us. We're building our own fare rules engine for the DEN-MSY pilot: same verdicts, but every verdict comes with human-readable explanation lines that agents can paste straight into the PNR. Ops greps logs for these exact lines, so the strings below are contract, not suggestion.

Ground rule: the engine NEVER reads a clock. Every decision derives from dates handed in explicitly (the booking/change date rides on the request). If LocalDate.now() shows up in review, the PR bounces. Dates render ISO (LocalDate.toString()), money renders as dollars like $199.00 / $0.05 (Locale.ROOT).

Build sibling .java files in this directory (no packages, no build tool, plain JDK, source-launcher friendly):

FareClass.java — public record FareClass(String code, long baseCents, int advancePurchaseDays, int minStayNights, boolean changeable, long changeFeeCents).

TripRequest.java — public record TripRequest(LocalDate bookingDate, LocalDate departure, LocalDate returnDate). returnDate null means one-way.

Decision.java — public record Decision(boolean eligible, List<String> explanations).

Quote.java — public record Quote(String fareCode, long priceCents, List<String> verdicts).

ChangeQuote.java — public record ChangeQuote(boolean allowed, long feeCents, long fareDifferenceCents, long totalDueCents, List<String> explanations).

FareRules.java — the engine, all static:

money(long cents) -> String: "$" + dollars + '.' + two-digit cents, e.g. 19900 -> "$199.00", 5 -> "$0.05". Locale.ROOT if you format.

evaluate(FareClass, TripRequest) -> Decision. Rule precedence is fixed and explanations appear in exactly this order:
1. booking-window (sanity, TERMINAL): if departure is before bookingDate the decision is ineligible with the single line "FAIL booking-window: departure <dep> is before booking date <book>" and NO further lines; else if returnDate is non-null and before departure, the single line "FAIL booking-window: return <ret> is before departure <dep>". Same-day departure and zero-night same-day return are fine.
2. advance-purchase: required = advancePurchaseDays. 0 -> "PASS advance-purchase: not required". Else days = calendar days from bookingDate to departure (ChronoUnit.DAYS); days >= required passes. Line: "PASS advance-purchase: needs 14 days, has 21" / "FAIL advance-purchase: needs 14 days, has 9" — always the word 'days', even for 1.
3. min-stay: required = minStayNights. 0 -> "PASS min-stay: not required". Else a one-way trip fails with "FAIL min-stay: requires a round trip"; otherwise nights = days from departure to returnDate; nights >= required passes. Line: "PASS min-stay: needs 7 nights, has 8" / "FAIL min-stay: needs 7 nights, has 3" — always 'nights'.
Eligible iff no FAIL line.

cheapestEligible(List<FareClass>, TripRequest) -> Quote. One verdict line per fare, input order: eligible -> "K14: eligible at $199.00" (base price); ineligible -> "K14: ineligible (advance-purchase)" where the parenthetical is the rule name of the FIRST failing rule (booking-window / advance-purchase / min-stay). Winner = lowest baseCents among eligible; ties break to the lexicographically smallest code. Append one final line: "selected K14 at $199.00", or "no eligible fare" when nothing qualifies (also the sole line for an empty fare list). Quote carries the winner's code and baseCents, or (null, 0) when there is no winner.

change(FareClass oldFare, FareClass newFare, LocalDate purchaseDate, TripRequest newTrip) -> ChangeQuote. newTrip.bookingDate() IS the change date. Precedence:
1. oldFare not changeable -> denied: ChangeQuote(false, 0, 0, 0, ["DENY change: fare Q00 does not permit changes"]) — single line, nothing else evaluated.
2. Re-validate the NEW fare as of the change date: evaluate(newFare, newTrip). Ineligible -> denied with "DENY change: fare Q00 fails its rules" followed by that evaluation's explanation lines verbatim (this is also how rebooking onto a departure before the change date gets rejected, via the booking-window line). All cents fields 0.
3. Otherwise allowed. Fee: if the change date equals purchaseDate we are inside the same-day void window — fee 0, line "WAIVE fee: change within the same-day void window"; else fee = oldFare.changeFeeCents with line "FEE change: $75.00" (a zero fee outside the void window still prints "FEE change: $0.00").
4. Fare difference: charged = max(0, newFare.baseCents - oldFare.baseCents). Upgrade -> "FARE-DIFFERENCE: $30.00"; zero-or-down -> "FARE-DIFFERENCE: $0.00 (no refund on downgrade)".
5. totalDue = fee + charged, final line "TOTAL DUE: $105.00".
Explanations for an allowed change are exactly: ["ALLOW change: K14 -> M21", <fee or waive line>, <fare-difference line>, <total line>].

TASK
`tempjanitor.sh` is our small cleanup utility for a per-job temporary directory. A recent safety review found that it can reclaim a directory while a process still has a file open below that directory. Repair that defect without weakening any of the existing safeguards or changing the command's interface or audit schema.

Invocation is `bash tempjanitor.sh [--dry-run] --root DIR --age SECONDS --owner UID --lock FILE --now EPOCH`. All value options are required, numeric values are unsigned decimal integers, unknown/missing arguments print the usage line to stderr and exit 64, and the root must be a real directory rather than `/` or a symlink. `--now` is deliberately explicit so scheduled runs and tests make the same age decision: an immediate child is old enough when its own mtime is at or before `EPOCH - SECONDS`.

The janitor considers only immediate children of DIR. A candidate may be reclaimed only when it and every entry below it are owned by UID and are on the same device as DIR. A top-level symlink is skipped, and directory walks must never follow nested symlinks or cross a filesystem boundary. If any process has the candidate itself, or any path below a candidate directory, open through `/proc/*/fd`, the entire candidate is skipped. The lock is a nonblocking `flock(1)` held for the complete scan; contention produces no audit records or candidate changes, prints `tempjanitor.sh: lock busy: FILE`, and exits 75.

Successful runs write deterministic JSON Lines to stdout: one candidate record per immediate child in byte-sorted path order, then one summary. Skip reasons are `symlink`, `filesystem`, `owner`, `young`, or `open`; eligible dry-run records use action `would_remove`, live records use `removed`, and eligible records include the sum of regular-file content bytes in that candidate without following links or crossing devices. Dry-run may create/open the lock file but cannot change the candidate tree. A second identical live run must be idempotent. Keep stderr empty on successful scans.

The protected harness uses fixed mtimes and a local fake `stat` boundary to exercise the same-device and ownership decisions without mounts or privileges. It also holds old top-level files and a descendant file open using real descriptors, including path-component boundary, trailing-newline, and literal ` (deleted)` suffix cases, verifies exact reclaimed bytes and tree contents, checks lock contention, dry-run behavior, symlink safety, byte-exact JSONL, and a no-op second run. Run `bash test_tempjanitor.sh`; do not modify the test.

TASK
Tooling ticket: build `rs-tomlite`, a lossless TOML-lite config parser/editor for our deploy tooling. Every existing library deserializes into structs and loses the file layout; we need the opposite — a line-preserving document model our bots can edit surgically, so config diffs stay reviewable. The crate ships with its acceptance suite (tests/parse.rs, tests/edit.rs) and no src/ — `cargo test --offline` fails to compile until you implement the library. Rust 2021, stdlib only. Never touch tests/, Cargo.toml, or .gitignore.

Grammar (deliberately a TOML subset; do not add features): a document is lines, each one of — blank; full-line comment (first non-whitespace char `#`); table header `[name]` where name is dot-separated segments, each segment matching `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+` (whitespace allowed just inside the brackets, none around dots, nothing but whitespace after `]`); or `key = value` with a bare key `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`. Keys before any header belong to the root table, named `""`. Values: strings `"..."` with exactly the escapes \" \\ \n \t \r; integers `[+-]?[0-9]+` (NO underscore separators); floats `[+-]?[0-9]+\.[0-9]+` only (digits required on both sides of the dot); `true`/`false`; flat arrays `[v, v]` of those scalars (no nested arrays, no trailing comma, `[]` ok). There are NO inline comments: any non-whitespace after a complete value is an error.

Public API (tests import `rs_tomlite::{Document, ParseError, ParseErrorKind, Value}`):
- `Value { Str(String), Int(i64), Float(f64), Bool(bool), Array(Vec<Value>) }` with Debug + Clone + PartialEq.
- `Document::parse(input: &str) -> Result<Document, ParseError>`.
- `ParseError { pub line: usize, pub kind: ParseErrorKind }` (1-based line), Debug + PartialEq, Display `line {n}: {message}`. `ParseErrorKind` with messages: `BadHeader` "malformed table header"; `DuplicateTable { name }` "duplicate table '{name}'" (same header twice, reported at the second); `BadKey` "malformed key"; `MissingEquals` "expected '=' after key"; `BadValue` "unrecognized value" (also for an empty value); `UnterminatedString` "unterminated string"; `BadEscape` "invalid escape sequence"; `DuplicateKey { key }` "duplicate key '{key}'" (same key twice in one table; same key in different tables is fine); `TrailingChars` "unexpected trailing characters".
- `render(&self) -> String` — must reproduce the parsed source BYTE-IDENTICALLY: comments, blank lines, eccentric spacing like `port   =   8080` or `host="a"`, and the presence/absence of a final newline all survive.
- `get(&self, table: &str, key: &str) -> Option<&Value>`; `tables(&self) -> Vec<String>` in document order with root `""` first only when it actually has keys; `keys(&self, table: &str) -> Vec<String>` in document order (unknown table -> empty).
- `set(&mut self, table: &str, key: &str, value: Value)` — the surgical editor. Existing key: rewrite exactly that one line to the canonical form `key = value`; every other line stays byte-identical. New key in an existing table: insert the canonical line directly after that table's last key line (directly after the header if it has none); for the root table with no keys yet, insert at the very top of the document. Unknown table: append at the end — one separating blank line first if the document's last line isn't blank (no padding on an empty document), then `[table]`, then the key line. Canonical value rendering: strings quoted with the five escapes; ints plain; floats always with a decimal point (8.0 renders `8.0`, never `8`); `true`/`false`; arrays `[a, b]` comma-space separated. set() must keep get/tables/keys and a later parse(render()) consistent.

Acceptance: `cargo test --offline` fully green (36 tests: 22 parse + 14 edit). Determinism throughout — no hash-map ordering may leak into tables(), keys(), or any error.

Every existing library deserializes into structs and loses the file layout; we need the opposite — a line-preserving document model our bots can edit surgically, so config diffs stay reviewable. Grammar (deliberately a TOML subset; do not add features): a document is lines, each one of — blank; full-line comment (first non-whitespace char `#`); table header `[name]` where name is dot-separated segments, each segment matching `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+` (whitespace allowed just inside the brackets, none around dots, nothing but whitespace after `]`); or `key = value` with a bare key `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`. Keys before any header belong to the root table, named `""`. Values: strings `"..."` with exactly the escapes \" \\ \n \t \r; integers `[+-]?[0-9]+` (NO underscore separators); floats `[+-]?[0-9]+\.[0-9]+` only (digits required on both sides of the dot); `true`/`false`; flat arrays `[v, v]` of those scalars (no nested arrays, no trailing comma, `[]` ok). There are NO inline comments: any non-whitespace after a complete value is an error.

Public API (tests import `rs_tomlite::{Document, ParseError, ParseErrorKind, Value}`):
- `Value { Str(String), Int(i64), Float(f64), Bool(bool), Array(Vec<Value>) }` with Debug + Clone + PartialEq.
- `Document::parse(input: &str) -> Result<Document, ParseError>`.
- `ParseError { pub line: usize, pub kind: ParseErrorKind }` (1-based line), Debug + PartialEq, Display `line {n}: {message}`. `ParseErrorKind` with messages: `BadHeader` "malformed table header"; `DuplicateTable { name }` "duplicate table '{name}'" (same header twice, reported at the second); `BadKey` "malformed key"; `MissingEquals` "expected '=' after key"; `BadValue` "unrecognized value" (also for an empty value); `UnterminatedString` "unterminated string"; `BadEscape` "invalid escape sequence"; `DuplicateKey { key }` "duplicate key '{key}'" (same key twice in one table; same key in different tables is fine); `TrailingChars` "unexpected trailing characters".
- `render(&self) -> String` — must reproduce the parsed source BYTE-IDENTICALLY: comments, blank lines, eccentric spacing like `port   =   8080` or `host="a"`, and the presence/absence of a final newline all survive.
- `get(&self, table: &str, key: &str) -> Option<&Value>`; `tables(&self) -> Vec<String>` in document order with root `""` first only when it actually has keys; `keys(&self, table: &str) -> Vec<String>` in document order (unknown table -> empty).
- `set(&mut self, table: &str, key: &str, value: Value)` — the surgical editor. Existing key: rewrite exactly that one line to the canonical form `key = value`; every other line stays byte-identical. New key in an existing table: insert the canonical line directly after that table's last key line (directly after the header if it has none); for the root table with no keys yet, insert at the very top of the document. Unknown table: append at the end — one separating blank line first if the document's last line isn't blank (no padding on an empty document), then `[table]`, then the key line. Tooling ticket: build `rs-tomlite`, a lossless TOML-lite config parser/editor for our deploy tooling. Every existing library deserializes into structs and loses the file layout; we need the opposite — a line-preserving document model our bots can edit surgically, so config diffs stay reviewable. The crate ships with its acceptance suite (tests/parse.rs, tests/edit.rs) and no src/ — `cargo test --offline` fails to compile until you implement the library. Rust 2021, stdlib only. Never touch tests/, Cargo.toml, or .gitignore.

Grammar (deliberately a TOML subset; do not add features): a document is lines, each one of — blank; full-line comment (first non-whitespace char `#`); table header `[name]` where name is dot-separated segments, each segment matching `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+` (whitespace allowed just inside the brackets, none around dots, nothing but whitespace after `]`); or `key = value` with a bare key `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`. Keys before any header belong to the root table, named `""`. Values: strings `"..."` with exactly the escapes \" \\ \n \t \r; integers `[+-]?[0-9]+` (NO underscore separators); floats `[+-]?[0-9]+\.[0-9]+` only (digits required on both sides of the dot); `true`/`false`; flat arrays `[v, v]` of those scalars (no nested arrays, no trailing comma, `[]` ok). There are NO inline comments: any non-whitespace after a complete value is an error.

Public API (tests import `rs_tomlite::{Document, ParseError, ParseErrorKind, Value}`):
- `Value { Str(String), Int(i64), Float(f64), Bool(bool), Array(Vec<Value>) }` with Debug + Clone + PartialEq.
- `Document::parse(input: &str) -> Result<Document, ParseError>`.
- `ParseError { pub line: usize, pub kind: ParseErrorKind }` (1-based line), Debug + PartialEq, Display `line {n}: {message}`. `ParseErrorKind` with messages: `BadHeader` "malformed table header"; `DuplicateTable { name }` "duplicate table '{name}'" (same header twice, reported at the second); `BadKey` "malformed key"; `MissingEquals` "expected '=' after key"; `BadValue` "unrecognized value" (also for an empty value); `UnterminatedString` "unterminated string"; `BadEscape` "invalid escape sequence"; `DuplicateKey { key }` "duplicate key '{key}'" (same key twice in one table; same key in different tables is fine); `TrailingChars` "unexpected trailing characters".
- `render(&self) -> String` — must reproduce the parsed source BYTE-IDENTICALLY: comments, blank lines, eccentric spacing like `port   =   8080` or `host="a"`, and the presence/absence of a final newline all survive.

New key in an existing table: insert the canonical line directly after that table's last key line (directly after the header if it has none); for the root table with no keys yet, insert at the very top of the document. Unknown table: append at the end — one separating blank line first if the document's last line isn't blank (no padding on an empty document), then `[table]`, then the key line. Files are ASCII with LF line endings. Splitting is dumb on purpose: N commas means N+1 fields, so `a,b,` is three fields with the third one empty. Cells keep their spaces verbatim — no trimming, and spaces count toward width.

Usage: `table.sh <file.csv> [maxwidth]`. maxwidth caps every column and defaults to 16; it must be a decimal integer >= 5, anything else gets `table.sh: maxwidth must be an integer >= 5` on stderr and exit 64 (validate it before touching the file). No arguments at all: `usage: table.sh <file.csv> [maxwidth]` on stderr, exit 64. Missing or unreadable file: `table.sh: cannot read: <arg>` on stderr, exit 66.

Rendering rules, and I mean them precisely:
- The first line is the header and fixes the column count C. Validate before you print anything: every data line must have exactly C fields; on the FIRST offender print `table.sh: line <N>: expected <C> fields, got <K>` to stderr (N is the 1-based physical line number) and exit 65 with NOTHING on stdout. A zero-line file: `table.sh: empty input` to stderr, exit 65.
- A column is numeric iff it has at least one data row AND every one of its data cells matches the ERE `^-?[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?$`. The header cell never counts, and an empty cell, `1e3`, ` 7`, `+5` all disqualify. Numeric columns right-align; everything else left-aligns; the header cell follows its column's alignment.
- Column width W = min(maxwidth, longest cell in the column, header included). Any cell longer than W renders as its first W-3 characters plus `...` — that is three ASCII dots, NOT a Unicode ellipsis; our terminals and diffs stay ASCII. Numeric detection looks at ORIGINAL cell values; truncation is display-only.
- Render: pad every cell to exactly W (left-pad when right-aligned, right-pad when left-aligned), join cells with ` | ` (space pipe space), then strip trailing spaces off each finished line — no output line ever ends in a space. After the header print a separator line: W dashes per column, columns joined with `-+-`. Data rows follow in input order. On success stderr stays empty and the exit code is 0. A header-only file renders header + separator and exits 0.
- Pure bash. Width math with `${#cell}`, padding with printf, reading with builtins. No awk, no column(1), no sed, no external commands for any of the rendering. (Pure bash also keeps it happy on the macOS boxes.)

widget,12,3.50,fast mover
long-tail adapter cable spool,3,17.25,check reorder threshold soon
gizmo,-4,0.99,

-----------------+-----+------------+-----------------
widget           |  12 |       3.50 | fast mover
long-tail ada... |   3 |      17.25 | check reorder...
gizmo            |  -4 |       0.99 |

About the input, so nobody gold-plates this: our exporter NEVER quotes. A comma is always a field separator, there is no escaping of any kind, and RFC-4180 quoted fields are explicitly OUT of scope — real CSV parsing lives elsewhere in the stack, this is a renderer. Files are ASCII with LF line endings. Splitting is dumb on purpose: N commas means N+1 fields, so `a,b,` is three fields with the third one empty. Cells keep their spaces verbatim — no trimming, and spaces count toward width.

Usage: `table.sh <file.csv> [maxwidth]`. maxwidth caps every column and defaults to 16; it must be a decimal integer >= 5, anything else gets `table.sh: maxwidth must be an integer >= 5` on stderr and exit 64 (validate it before touching the file). No arguments at all: `usage: table.sh <file.csv> [maxwidth]` on stderr, exit 64. Missing or unreadable file: `table.sh: cannot read: <arg>` on stderr, exit 66.

Rendering rules, and I mean them precisely:
- The first line is the header and fixes the column count C. Validate before you print anything: every data line must have exactly C fields; on the FIRST offender print `table.sh: line <N>: expected <C> fields, got <K>` to stderr (N is the 1-based physical line number) and exit 65 with NOTHING on stdout. A zero-line file: `table.sh: empty input` to stderr, exit 65.
- A column is numeric iff it has at least one data row AND every one of its data cells matches the ERE `^-?[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?$`. The header cell never counts, and an empty cell, `1e3`, ` 7`, `+5` all disqualify. Numeric columns right-align; everything else left-aligns; the header cell follows its column's alignment.
- Column width W = min(maxwidth, longest cell in the column, header included). Any cell longer than W renders as its first W-3 characters plus `...` — that is three ASCII dots, NOT a Unicode ellipsis; our terminals and diffs stay ASCII. Numeric detection looks at ORIGINAL cell values; truncation is display-only.
- Render: pad every cell to exactly W (left-pad when right-aligned, right-pad when left-aligned), join cells with ` | ` (space pipe space), then strip trailing spaces off each finished line — no output line ever ends in a space. After the header print a separator line: W dashes per column, columns joined with `-+-`. Data rows follow in input order. On success stderr stays empty and the exit code is 0. A header-only file renders header + separator and exits 0.
- Pure bash. Width math with `${#cell}`, padding with printf, reading with builtins. No awk, no column(1), no sed, no external commands for any of the rendering. (Pure bash also keeps it happy on the macOS boxes.)

About the input, so nobody gold-plates this: our exporter NEVER quotes. A comma is always a field separator, there is no escaping of any kind, and RFC-4180 quoted fields are explicitly OUT of scope — real CSV parsing lives elsewhere in the stack, this is a renderer. Files are ASCII with LF line endings. Splitting is dumb on purpose: N commas means N+1 fields, so `a,b,` is three fields with the third one empty. Cells keep their spaces verbatim — no trimming, and spaces count toward width.

Usage: `table.sh <file.csv> [maxwidth]`. maxwidth caps every column and defaults to 16; it must be a decimal integer >= 5, anything else gets `table.sh: maxwidth must be an integer >= 5` on stderr and exit 64 (validate it before touching the file). No arguments at all: `usage: table.sh <file.csv> [maxwidth]` on stderr, exit 64. Missing or unreadable file: `table.sh: cannot read: <arg>` on stderr, exit 66.

Rendering rules, and I mean them precisely:
- The first line is the header and fixes the column count C. Validate before you print anything: every data line must have exactly C fields; on the FIRST offender print `table.sh: line <N>: expected <C> fields, got <K>` to stderr (N is the 1-based physical line number) and exit 65 with NOTHING on stdout. A zero-line file: `table.sh: empty input` to stderr, exit 65.
- A column is numeric iff it has at least one data row AND every one of its data cells matches the ERE `^-?[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?$`. The header cell never counts, and an empty cell, `1e3`, ` 7`, `+5` all disqualify. Numeric columns right-align; everything else left-aligns; the header cell follows its column's alignment.
- Column width W = min(maxwidth, longest cell in the column, header included). Any cell longer than W renders as its first W-3 characters plus `...` — that is three ASCII dots, NOT a Unicode ellipsis; our terminals and diffs stay ASCII. Numeric detection looks at ORIGINAL cell values; truncation is display-only.
- Render: pad every cell to exactly W (left-pad when right-aligned, right-pad when left-aligned), join cells with ` | ` (space pipe space), then strip trailing spaces off each finished line — no output line ever ends in a space. After the header print a separator line: W dashes per column, columns joined with `-+-`. Data rows follow in input order. On success stderr stays empty and the exit code is 0. A header-only file renders header + separator and exits 0.
- Pure bash. Width math with `${#cell}`, padding with printf, reading with builtins. No awk, no column(1), no sed, no external commands for any of the rendering. (Pure bash also keeps it happy on the macOS boxes.)

A comma is always a field separator, there is no escaping of any kind, and RFC-4180 quoted fields are explicitly OUT of scope — real CSV parsing lives elsewhere in the stack, this is a renderer. Files are ASCII with LF line endings. Splitting is dumb on purpose: N commas means N+1 fields, so `a,b,` is three fields with the third one empty. Cells keep their spaces verbatim — no trimming, and spaces count toward width.

Usage: `table.sh <file.csv> [maxwidth]`. maxwidth caps every column and defaults to 16; it must be a decimal integer >= 5, anything else gets `table.sh: maxwidth must be an integer >= 5` on stderr and exit 64 (validate it before touching the file). No arguments at all: `usage: table.sh <file.csv> [maxwidth]` on stderr, exit 64. Missing or unreadable file: `table.sh: cannot read: <arg>` on stderr, exit 66.

Rendering rules, and I mean them precisely:
- The first line is the header and fixes the column count C. Validate before you print anything: every data line must have exactly C fields; on the FIRST offender print `table.sh: line <N>: expected <C> fields, got <K>` to stderr (N is the 1-based physical line number) and exit 65 with NOTHING on stdout. A zero-line file: `table.sh: empty input` to stderr, exit 65.
- A column is numeric iff it has at least one data row AND every one of its data cells matches the ERE `^-?[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?$`. The header cell never counts, and an empty cell, `1e3`, ` 7`, `+5` all disqualify. Numeric columns right-align; everything else left-aligns; the header cell follows its column's alignment.
- Column width W = min(maxwidth, longest cell in the column, header included). Any cell longer than W renders as its first W-3 characters plus `...` — that is three ASCII dots, NOT a Unicode ellipsis; our terminals and diffs stay ASCII. Numeric detection looks at ORIGINAL cell values; truncation is display-only.
- Render: pad every cell to exactly W (left-pad when right-aligned, right-pad when left-aligned), join cells with ` | ` (space pipe space), then strip trailing spaces off each finished line — no output line ever ends in a space. After the header print a separator line: W dashes per column, columns joined with `-+-`. Data rows follow in input order. On success stderr stays empty and the exit code is 0. A header-only file renders header + separator and exits 0.
- Pure bash. Width math with `${#cell}`, padding with printf, reading with builtins. No awk, no column(1), no sed, no external commands for any of the rendering. (Pure bash also keeps it happy on the macOS boxes.)
